summary: This experimental TLS extension carries in-band the full set of DNSSEC-validatable records needed to do DANE for a TLS server, removing separate DNS lookups. If records do not exist, it conveys a denial-of-existence proof. It was developed outside the IETF and published to guide interoperable implementations.

eli5.summary: When a website shows its ID, it can also bring the proof from the phone book so you do not have to look it up yourself. This experiment does that.

subtitle: Carrying DNS security proofs inside the TLS handshake

tldr.problem: DANE authentication of TLS servers requires DNS lookups for DNSSEC-signed records, but clients may not have access to DNS or may not trust their resolver, creating a chicken-and-egg problem and additional latency.
tldr.mechanism: A TLS extension lets servers include the complete chain of DNSSEC-signed DNS records and signatures needed to authenticate the server's identity, eliminating the need for out-of-band DNS lookups.
tldr.outcome: TLS clients can now perform DANE authentication without trusting their local DNS resolver, and DNS-over-TLS connections can bootstrap themselves. The document is Experimental to study real-world deployments.

today: RFC 9102 is an Experimental specification published in August 2021, developed outside the IETF for interoperability. Adoption has been limited so far. The Experimental status allows real-world deployment experience to inform whether a Standards Track version is appropriate.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
DANE (DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities) lets a TLS server prove its identity using records in the DNS, signed with DNSSEC. A client validates the DNS records and then uses them to authenticate the server's certificate. This solves a long-standing problem in TLS: how to verify a server's certificate without relying on a centralized certificate authority.

The catch: to do DANE, the client must perform separate DNS lookups and validate DNSSEC signatures. If the client does not have access to a validating DNS resolver, or does not trust it (as is the case with DNS-over-TLS), it cannot perform DANE authentication at all. This RFC solves the problem by letting the TLS server send the DNSSEC-signed DNS records directly in the TLS handshake, carrying the proof in-band.
sections.eli5: A server can prove who it is using special DNS records instead of certificate authorities. But getting those records from DNS can be hard. This RFC lets the server send the records inside the connection handshake instead.

sections.title: How the Extension Works
sections.content:
The extension uses a two-part negotiation. The client sends a dnssec_chain extension in the TLS ClientHello, along with the SNI (Server Name Indication) hostname and a port number. The server, if it supports the extension and has configured DANE records for that hostname and port, responds with the extension containing the full DNSSEC authentication chain: the TLSA record (if it exists) or a proof of non-existence, plus all the intermediate DNS records and signatures needed to validate up the chain to a trust anchor, typically the root zone.

The server constructs the chain by querying DNS or retrieving it from cache, uncompresses any DNS name compression, and serializes the records in wire format. The response includes an ExtSupportLifetime value—the number of hours the server commits to serving this extension. A value of zero means the server makes no commitment; non-zero values enable a security feature called extension pinning (see below).
sections.eli5: The client asks 'send me the proof' and the server sends the whole chain of DNS records it got from the directory, all signed and ready to check.

sections.title: Building, Caching, and Validating Chains
sections.content:
The server's job is to construct and maintain the authentication chain. It starts with the TLSA record corresponding to the server's domain, protocol, and port, then walks the DNS tree upward toward the root, collecting DNSKEY and DS records at each zone cut along with their DNSSEC signatures. The server should cache this chain and refresh it as DNS TTLs require, rebuilding periodically rather than on every connection to minimize overhead.

On the client side, validation is straightforward: use DNSSEC validation to authenticate the chain, then apply DANE authentication rules to verify the server's certificate against the TLSA records. A client that receives a valid authentication chain MAY cache the TLSA records to amortize the cost of validation over multiple connections, but MUST respect the TTL values in the cached records.
sections.eli5: The server keeps the DNS records ready to send and updates them when they expire. The client receives them, checks the signatures to make sure they are real, then uses them to check the server's certificate.

sections.title: Extension Pinning and Downgrade Protection
sections.content:
A client might be subject to a downgrade attack: a man-in-the-middle intercepts the connection and presents a certificate that is valid under the WebPKI but not under DANE. To defend against this, the RFC defines extension pinning. When a client receives the extension with a non-zero ExtSupportLifetime and a valid TLSA authentication chain, it can 'pin' that server, recording the commitment. On future connections, the client requires the server to send the extension again; if the server omits it, the client aborts the connection rather than falling back to PKIX authentication.

Pinning is particularly important in deployments that mix PKIX and DANE authentication. A client with a cached TLSA RRset and an active pin MUST request the extension on the next connection, and if the server fails to respond with valid chain data, the client MUST either abort or attempt to fetch the records out-of-band. The ExtSupportLifetime is independent of DNS TTLs and signature expiration—it is purely the server's commitment to supporting the extension.
sections.eli5: If a server sends the proof once and promises to keep sending it, a client can remember that promise. On the next visit, if the proof is missing, the client knows something is wrong and stops, refusing to fall back to the old way of checking certificates.

sections.title: Deployment and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Servers must carefully manage the authentication chain to ensure it stays valid. Records with very short TTLs present a challenge; servers can serve the chain a few seconds beyond the minimum TTL to allow batch processing. Servers that manage virtual hosting must coordinate with domain owners before setting non-zero extension lifetimes, since an owner may wish to move services between providers. When CNAME records are involved (as in hosted services), the server uses the client's original SNI name for TLSA lookups, not any CNAME expansion, to avoid confusion.

A server wishing to stop supporting the extension must first advertise a zero ExtSupportLifetime, wait for all pinned clients to notice, and only then disable the extension. Clients need to keep their DNSSEC trust anchors up to date using mechanisms like RFC 5011 for automated key rollover. The RFC notes that the core mechanics are straightforward, but careful operational planning is essential for deployed services.
sections.eli5: Servers need to keep the DNS records fresh and ready to send. When they want to stop using this, they have to warn clients first so the clients do not expect it anymore.
